doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Optimism and the state of America
summary: Asked if she is optimistic, she speaks about slavery, genocide, greed, immigrants and how this shaped her need to help.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Do you consider yourself an optimist?
I thought you’d say oh yes. This is a little off topic, but does your optimism include the wider view of our country at the moment?

Woo. Bigger question. Let’s put it this way. I believe that there are consequences for all actions and this country was founded on not just racism but murder, but stolen lives. Stolen, I mean this was based on genocide. Ten million natives who had been here for a hundred thousand years were murdered because we had a gun and they didn’t you know. Because we did not adapt to their ways, instead we forced our way on them. And ironically under the guise of Christianity you know, that has always been the way of early America and then there was slavery. Not even offering people a chance to come to a new country and make a living for you and your family. Think of the mindset. It was to capture other human beings, bring them here over an ocean in those days. Think about that. Whether they lived or died, and then sell them off and use them as property and beat them and kill them and rape them. I’m sorry to list it in such an upsetting manner but that was the truth of how industry grew. And as Danny Glover always taught me, you know it was the cotton gin, the cotton mill. That machine is what is responsible for slavery. Mass production is what caused all that to happen again but really the thing that comes before that is greed. You know? What I love is indigenous people believe that greed was a © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

mental illness, an affliction. If you ever hunted or took more than what your family or you needed, that was considered mental illness. They worried about that tribal member if he was ever taking more than what he needed. Land could never be owned. You know? I mean look at the way this country developed. And if you think it’s much different now, it’s not. Look what’s happening. People are being kidnapped off the streets. People who four years ago during the pandemic who were the heroes of the pandemic? It was immigrant workers were delivering the groceries. Immigrant workers were delivering Amazon so people could stay home and save their lives. They were putting their life on the line you know. Who does the work that no one else is willing to do in America? And now you’re putting that level of fear into our communities? Killing citizens who are standing up for them? I mean it’s beyond insane. So to be optimistic in a moment like this is like – it’s the original – I’m sorry – but it’s the original pain I had growing up of what happened in slavery, what happened in this country, what happened to indigenous people. As a kid we learned about them in school and it broke my heart then. And I think that was part of my need to want to help anyone from those communities that suffered from that original feeling of like what could I do. I couldn’t do anything from 200 years ago, or 100 years ago, or 60 years ago, but maybe you know there was a part of me that –
Well you’ve certainly made good on your passion and your humanity. And am I correct that you’re still doing it in your new location?
